front: You are a Python quant. In Python, b = a makes both names refer to one list, so b.append(4) also changes a. What does the C++ equivalent do with std::vector<int> b = a; b.push_back(4);, and what are the three default mental-model differences from Python you must internalise?
back:
Headline: in C++ = copies the whole object by default. Python binds a second name to the same object; C++ shares only through an explicit & or pointer.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> a{1, 2, 3};
    std::vector<int> b = a;     // copies all elements
    b.push_back(4);
    std::cout << a.size() << ' ' << b.size() << '\n';
}
Output: 3 4 (a is unchanged).

Three defaults to internalise:
  • Static types: every variable has a type fixed at compile time; the compiler rejects int x = "hi"; before the program runs.
  • No garbage collector: an automatic object is destroyed when execution leaves its scope. Heap memory is released by its owner, usually a std::vector or std::unique_ptr, not by a collector.
  • Value semantics: assignment and by-value parameters copy the object. Sharing needs & or a pointer.
Interview trap: the Python habit of passing containers around freely becomes a silent deep copy here. The compiler does not warn about it.

front: In C++ every variable's type is fixed at {{c1::compile time}}, so int x = "hi"; is rejected before the program runs. C++ has no {{c2::garbage collector}}: an object with automatic storage is destroyed when execution leaves its {{c3::scope}}.
back: Python allows x = 1; x = "hi" because a name is a binding to a typed object, and the binding can change. In C++ the variable is the typed storage itself.

front: Walk through what happens between main.cpp and an executable for g++ -std=c++20 main.cpp other.cpp -o app. Name each stage, the artefact it produces, and which stage reports each kind of error.
back:
1. Preprocessor: expands #include (a textual paste of the header), #define, and #if. Output: one translation unit (TU) per .cpp. Inspect with g++ -E.
  2. Compiler: parses and type-checks each TU, optimises it, and emits machine code. Syntax and type errors come from here. Each TU is compiled separately; -c stops here and writes .o.
  3. Assembler: turns assembly (-S) into an object file that contains defined symbols and a list of unresolved references.
  4. Linker: matches every reference to exactly one definition across all object files and libraries and writes the executable. undefined reference and multiple definition come from here.
A header's text is compiled once in every .cpp that includes it. Changing a header recompiles all its includers; changing a .cpp recompiles only that file, then relinks.

Interview trap: a missing semicolon is a compile error and stops at stage 2. A missing function body is a link error at stage 4, after every file compiled cleanly.

front: What goes in a header and what goes in a .cpp file? Why does a header hold declarations, and what does #include "x.hpp" actually do?
back:
Headline: #include is a textual paste done by the preprocessor. The header lets every TU see the same declarations.

  • Declaration says a name exists and gives its type: double discount_factor(double r, double t);. It can appear any number of times.
  • Definition gives the body or storage. An ordinary function or non-inline variable must be defined in exactly one TU.
  • Headers hold: declarations, class definitions (the compiler needs the layout for sizeof and members), inline and template functions (their bodies must be visible wherever they are used), and constexpr functions.
  • .cpp files hold: ordinary function bodies and variable definitions.
Interview trap: putting a non-inline function body in a header breaks the one-definition rule the moment two .cpp files include it (card on ODR below).

front: A header included twice in one translation unit is protected by an include guard: #ifndef RATES_HPP, #define RATES_HPP, body, #endif. #pragma once does the same job and is {{c1::supported by all major compilers but is not part of the ISO standard}}. Without a guard, a class defined twice in one TU gives a {{c2::redefinition}} error.
back: Guards stop a second copy of the text within a single TU. They do nothing about the same function defined in two different .cpp files; that is a linker problem (ODR).

front: What is the minimal C++ program that prints to stdout? Compile it with g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 and state the output. Then explain what int main() must return and what happens if you write void main().
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "Hello, rates desk\n";
    return 0;
}
Output: Hello, rates desk

  • <iostream> provides std::cout. << is the insertion operator.
  • main must return int. The value is the process exit status. If you reach the closing brace of main, it returns 0 automatically; no other function gets that treatment.
  • void main() is rejected by g++:
    main.cpp:3:1: error: ‘::main’ must return ‘int’
    3 | void main() {
      | ^~~~
Interview trap: std::endl also flushes the stream, which is expensive inside a loop. Use '\n' unless you need the flush.

front: A translation unit calls df(0.05, 1.0), and df is declared in a header but never defined. The compiler is happy and the linker fails with undefined reference to 'df(double, double)'. What causes this, and how do you fix it?
back:
double df(double r, double t);   // declared, never defined

int main() {
    return df(0.05, 1.0) > 0 ? 0 : 1;
}
g++ output:
/usr/bin/ld: <obj>: in function `main':
main.cpp:(.text.startup+0x19): undefined reference to `df(double, double)'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
Cause: the compiler checked the declaration; the linker found no object file or library that defines the symbol.

Fixes:
  • Define df in a .cpp and add that file to the build command (or its .o).
  • Link the library that defines it, e.g. -L/path -lpricing.
  • Check the signature. C++ mangles the parameter types into the symbol name, so df(double) and df(double,double) are different symbols. Linking C code also needs extern "C" on the declaration.
Interview trap: a signature mismatch produces exactly this error even when the function exists. Compare the mangled names with nm -C.

front: The header dup.hpp contains double bump(double x) { return x + 1e-4; } with no inline. Two .cpp files include it and the program is linked. What happens, and which rule does it break?
back:
Rule: the One Definition Rule (ODR). Each non-inline function or variable with external linkage must be defined exactly once in the whole program.

dup.hpp
#pragma once
double bump(double x) { return x + 1e-4; }   // non-inline definition in a header
a.cpp
#include "dup.hpp"
double fa() { return bump(1.0); }
main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include "dup.hpp"
double fa();
int main() { std::cout << fa() + bump(2.0) << '\n'; }
Linker output:
/usr/bin/ld: <obj>: in function `bump(double)':
a.cpp:(.text+0x0): multiple definition of `bump(double)'; <obj>:main.cpp:(.text+0x0): first defined here
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
Each TU receives its own copy of the header text, so each object file contains a definition of bump.

Fixes: declare in the header and define in one .cpp; or mark the function inline, which permits identical definitions in every TU. Templates and constexpr functions are implicitly inline.

Interview trap: the linker reports only duplicate external symbols. Many ODR violations, such as two different classes with the same name, link silently.

front: Write the header/source split for a discount factor discount_factor(r, t) = e^{-rt} (continuous compounding). Give the header, the source, and a main that prints discount_factor(0.05, 2.0). What does it print, and what build commands do you use?
back:
discount.hpp
#pragma once
// Discount factor for a continuously compounded rate r over t years.
double discount_factor(double r, double t);
discount.cpp
#include "discount.hpp"
#include <cmath>

double discount_factor(double r, double t) {
    return std::exp(-r * t);
}
main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include "discount.hpp"

int main() {
    std::cout << discount_factor(0.05, 2.0) << '\n';
}
Build: g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -c discount.cpp, then g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 main.cpp discount.o -o split.
Output: 0.904837 (that is \(e^{-0.1}\) to six significant digits).

The header carries only the declaration, so <cmath> stays in the .cpp and each include is cheap. A change to the .cpp rebuilds one object file.

Interview trap: the call compiles with the arguments swapped. discount_factor(2.0, 0.05) returns the same value because the product \(rt\) is symmetric. The compiler checks types, not meaning; name parameters clearly and keep units in the name, e.g. r_cont, t_years.

front: On this Linux x86-64 build, what are sizeof(int), sizeof(long) and sizeof(double)? Which sizes does the standard guarantee and which are platform-specific? What does --u do to unsigned int u = 0?
back:
#include <climits>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::cout << "char      " << sizeof(char) << '\n';
    std::cout << "int       " << sizeof(int) << '\n';
    std::cout << "long      " << sizeof(long) << '\n';
    std::cout << "long long " << sizeof(long long) << '\n';
    std::cout << "double    " << sizeof(double) << '\n';
    std::cout << "INT_MAX   " << INT_MAX << '\n';
    unsigned int u = 0;
    --u;
    std::cout << "0u - 1    " << u << '\n';
    std::int64_t big = 3000000000LL;
    std::cout << "int64 3e9 " << big << '\n';
}
Output:
char 1
int 4
long 8
long long 8
double 8
INT_MAX 2147483647
0u - 1 4294967295
int64 3e9 3000000000

  • The standard fixes sizeof(char) == 1 and sets minimum widths only (e.g. int at least 16 bits, long at least 32, long long at least 64).
  • Unsigned arithmetic is modular: 0u - 1 equals \(2^{32}-1\) = 4294967295 for a 32-bit unsigned int.
  • Use std::int64_t from <cstdint> when the width matters.
Interview trap: long is 8 bytes on Linux (LP64) and 4 bytes on 64-bit Windows (LLP64). A trade counter stored in long changes range across platforms. Signed overflow is a different matter: it is undefined behaviour (see the UB cards).

front: What do these lines print: 7 / 2, 7 / 2.0, -7 / 2, -7 % 3? How do they differ from Python's // and %?
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 7, b = 2;
    std::cout << a / b << '\n';                       // 3
    std::cout << 7 / 2.0 << '\n';                     // 3.5
    std::cout << static_cast<double>(a) / b << '\n';  // 3.5
    std::cout << -7 / 2 << '\n';                      // -3: truncates toward zero
    std::cout << -7 % 3 << '\n';                      // -1: sign follows dividend
}
Output (one per line): 3 , 3.5 , 3.5 , -3 , -1

Rules (C++11 and later): integer division truncates toward zero, and the sign of % follows the dividend. (a / b) * b + a % b == a always holds.
Python: 7 // 2 == 3 as in C++, but -7 // 2 == -4 (floor) and -7 % 3 == 2 (sign of the divisor).

Interview trap: double x = 7 / 2; gives 3.0, because the division happens on ints before the conversion. Bucketing a negative quantity with integer division rounds toward zero, not down; use std::floor on a double when you need floor semantics.

front: What is wrong with int n{3.7};, while int m = 3.7; compiles? Give the g++ error and the rule behind it. Then give the surprising behaviour of std::vector<int> v{5} versus v(5).
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int n{3.7};          // narrowing double -> int inside braces
    std::cout << n << '\n';
}
g++ error:
main.cpp: In function ‘int main()’:
main.cpp:4:11: error: narrowing conversion of ‘3.7000000000000002e+0’ from ‘double’ to ‘int’ [-Wnarrowing]
    4 |     int n{3.7};          // narrowing double -> int inside braces
      |           ^~~
Rule: list-initialisation (braces) rejects narrowing conversions that can lose value: floating to integer, and wider to narrower integer when the value may not fit. Copy-initialisation with = truncates silently: int m = 3.7; gives 3.

Interview trap: std::vector<int> v1{5} is one element holding 5; std::vector<int> v2(5) is five zeros. Braces prefer the initializer-list constructor. Output of the same comparison:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v1{5};     // list-initialisation: one element, value 5
    std::vector<int> v2(5);     // parentheses: five elements, each 0
    std::cout << v1.size() << ' ' << v1[0] << " | " << v2.size() << ' ' << v2[0] << '\n';
}
1 5 | 5 0

front: What type does auto deduce in each case: auto a = pillars; with const std::vector<double> pillars; const auto& r = pillars;; auto x = 2.0f;? How can you check the answer at compile time?
back:
#include <type_traits>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const std::vector<double> pillars{0.5, 1.0};
    auto a = pillars;                       // top-level const dropped: std::vector<double>
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(a), std::vector<double>>);
    const auto& r = pillars;                // const reference, no copy
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(r), const std::vector<double>&>);
    auto x = 2.0f;                          // float
    static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(x), float>);
    return static_cast<int>(a.size()) - 2;  // 0
}
Compiles with no diagnostics. The static_asserts are checked by the compiler; the run gives exit=0.

  • auto a = pillars; is std::vector<double>: top-level const is dropped and the object is copied.
  • const auto& r is a const std::vector<double>&: no copy.
  • auto x = 2.0f; is float.
Interview trap: auto x = 0; is int, not double. Writing auto a = container; on a large object is a silent deep copy; write const auto& when you only read.

front: auto deduces the type from the initialiser using template argument deduction. Top-level {{c1::const}} and {{c2::reference}} qualifiers are dropped, so auto a = ref_to_const; yields a {{c3::copy}}. Write {{c4::const auto&}} to bind to the original without copying.
back: The type is decided once, at the initialiser. auto x = 1; is int; auto y = 1.0; is double. Both are fixed for their lifetime.

front: What is the difference between const and constexpr? Give an example where a constexpr function is checked at compile time, and state what the program prints.
back:
#include <iostream>

constexpr double bp = 1e-4;                                  // compile-time constant
constexpr double df_const(double r, double t) { return 1.0 / (1.0 + r * t); }
static_assert(df_const(0.0, 5.0) == 1.0);                    // evaluated by the compiler

int main() {
    const double notional = 1e6;                             // read-only at run time
    double dv01 = notional * bp;
    std::cout << bp << ' ' << dv01 << '\n';
}
Output: 0.0001 100

  • const means the object cannot be modified after initialisation. Its value may be known only at run time.
  • constexpr requires the value to be a compile-time constant. A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time when all its inputs are constant expressions. The same function still runs at run time with run-time arguments.
  • static_assert(df_const(0.0, 5.0) == 1.0) is evaluated by the compiler; a false condition is a compile error.
Interview trap: const double x = f(v); compiles for any v. constexpr double x = f(v); fails unless v is a constant expression.

front: Compare references and pointers: declaration syntax, null, rebinding, and what r = y; does when r refers to x. Trace the code and give the printed output.
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int x = 1, y = 2;
    int& r = x;          // must be bound at declaration, cannot be null
    r = 10;              // writes x
    int* p = nullptr;    // pointers can be null
    int* q = &x;
    q = &y;              // pointer rebinding is allowed
    *q = 20;             // writes y
    r = y;               // NOT a rebind: copies y's value into x
    std::cout << x << ' ' << y << ' ' << (p == nullptr) << '\n';
}
Output: 20 20 1

Trace: x=1, y=2. r = 10 writes x. q = &y rebinds the pointer. *q = 20 writes y. r = y copies y's value (20) into x.

  • A reference must be bound when declared, is an alias for its target, and cannot be null.
  • A pointer can be null (nullptr) and can be reassigned to point elsewhere.
Interview trap: r = y; looks like rebinding if you think in Python. There is no rebinding of a reference: it assigns through the alias.

front: For a large object such as a Curve holding a vector of pillars, should the function take it by value, by non-const reference, or by const&? Show the copy count for the first two calls in this program.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Curve {
    std::vector<double> pillars;
    Curve() = default;
    Curve(const Curve& o) : pillars(o.pillars) { ++copies; }
    static inline int copies = 0;
};

double by_value(Curve c)          { return static_cast<double>(c.pillars.size()); }
double by_cref(const Curve& c)    { return static_cast<double>(c.pillars.size()); }

int main() {
    Curve c;
    c.pillars.assign(1000, 1.0);
    by_value(c);
    std::cout << "after by value: " << Curve::copies << '\n';
    by_cref(c);
    std::cout << "after const&:   " << Curve::copies << '\n';
}
Output:
after by value: 1
after const&: 1

Answer: const Curve&. It is read-only, copies nothing, and binds to both lvalues and temporaries. A non-const Curve& rejects temporaries and invites mutation. By value copies the whole container (here a heap allocation of 1000 doubles) unless the function needs its own copy to store or modify.

Interview trap: const& is safe only while the referred object lives. Storing it in a member or a lambda that outlives the call creates a dangling reference.

front: What does this print and why: set_by_value(int x) { x = 5; }, set_by_ref(int& x) { x = 5; }, set_ptr(int* p) { *p = 5; }, called on a, b, c, all initialised to 1?
back:
#include <iostream>

void set_by_value(int x) { x = 5; }
void set_by_ref(int& x)  { x = 5; }
void set_ptr(int* p)     { *p = 5; }

int main() {
    int a = 1, b = 1, c = 1;
    set_by_value(a);
    set_by_ref(b);
    set_ptr(&c);
    std::cout << a << ' ' << b << ' ' << c << '\n';
}
Output: 1 5 5

The by-value call changes only its local copy. The reference and pointer calls write to the caller's object. g++ also warns that the parameter x in set_by_value is set but never used, because the write has no visible effect.

Interview trap: in C++ the caller cannot tell from the call site whether an argument may change. The signature (int, int&, int*, const int&) carries that contract; Python has no equivalent.

front: What do these calls select and print: show(2), show(2.0), show('A') with overloads for int and double; and df(0.05, 1.0) versus df(0.05, 1.0, 0.01) where df has a default third argument?
back:
#include <iostream>

double df(double r, double t, double spread = 0.0) {
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + (r + spread) * t);
}
void show(int x)    { std::cout << "int " << x << '\n'; }
void show(double x) { std::cout << "double " << x << '\n'; }

int main() {
    show(2);
    show(2.0);
    show('A');                 // char promotes to int: exact match after promotion
    std::cout << df(0.05, 1.0) << ' ' << df(0.05, 1.0, 0.01) << '\n';
}
Output:
int 2
double 2
int 65
0.952381 0.943396

Overload resolution: an exact match beats a promotion (char to int, float to double), which beats a standard conversion (int to double). 'A' is promoted to int and prints 65.
Default arguments are part of the declaration and are substituted at the call site. Repeat them only in the header, never in the definition.

Interview trap: unlike Python's default arguments, C++ defaults are not evaluated once and shared, so the mutable-default bug does not exist. Their resolution is static.

front: Why does price(100) fail to compile when both void price(int, double = 0.0) and void price(int) are declared? Give the compiler message and two fixes.
back:
#include <iostream>

void price(int notional, double spread = 0.0) {
    std::cout << notional << ' ' << spread << '\n';
}
void price(int notional) {
    std::cout << "no spread " << notional << '\n';
}

int main() {
    price(100);
}
g++ error:
main.cpp: In function ‘int main()’:
main.cpp:11:10: error: call of overloaded ‘price(int)’ is ambiguous
   11 |     price(100);
      |     ~~~~~^~~~~
main.cpp:3:6: note: candidate: ‘void price(int, double)’
    3 | void price(int notional, double spread = 0.0) {
      |      ^~~~~
main.cpp:6:6: note: candidate: ‘void price(int)’
    6 | void price(int notional) {
      |      ^~~~~
Both overloads are viable with identical conversions for price(100). The default argument makes the first one viable with one argument, so neither is better: the call is ambiguous.

Fixes: keep only one overload (the one with the default), or give the variant a distinct name such as price_with_spread.

Interview trap: adding a defaulted parameter to an existing pricing function can make existing calls ambiguous once an overload of the same name exists. Overload sets are a common source of silent behaviour changes in shared libraries.

front: This compiles with a warning. What is wrong, what happens at run time, and how do you fix it? const double& discount(double r) { double df = 1.0 / (1.0 + r); return df; }
back:
#include <iostream>

const double& discount(double r) {
    double df = 1.0 / (1.0 + r);   // local object
    return df;                      // reference to an object that dies on return
}

int main() {
    std::cout << discount(0.05) << '\n';
}
g++ warning:
main.cpp: In function ‘const double& discount(double)’:
main.cpp:5:12: warning: reference to local variable ‘df’ returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]
    5 |     return df;                      // reference to an object that dies on return
      |            ^~
main.cpp:4:12: note: declared here
    4 |     double df = 1.0 / (1.0 + r);   // local object
      |            ^~
What is wrong: df has automatic storage and is destroyed when discount returns. The caller receives a reference to dead storage; using it is undefined behaviour. On this build the program segfaults (exit code 139) at both -O0 and -O2; the failure is not guaranteed to look like that.

Fix: return the double by value. For a scalar that costs nothing, and for an object a return by value is also fine (copy elision, see the return-by-value card).

Interview trap: returning a reference to a member of a temporary is the same bug, and g++ warns only for direct locals such as this one.

front: Why can const double kBp = 1e-4; sit in a header included by many .cpp files, while double kScale = 1.0; in the same header causes a multiple-definition link error? What is the C++17 fix for kScale, and what does the fixed version print?
back:
rates.hpp
#pragma once
const double kBp = 1e-4;     // const at namespace scope: internal linkage, safe in a header
double kScale = 1.0;         // external linkage: a definition in every TU that includes it
a.cpp
#include "rates.hpp"
double fa() { return kBp * kScale; }
main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include "rates.hpp"
double fa();
int main() { std::cout << fa() << '\n'; }
Link error:
/usr/bin/ld: <obj>:(.data+0x0): multiple definition of `kScale'; <obj>:(.data+0x0): first defined here
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
Why: a namespace-scope const (or constexpr) object has internal linkage, so each TU gets a private copy and nothing clashes. A non-const variable has external linkage and must be defined once.

Fix (C++17): inline double kScale = 1.0; in the header. One shared object is used by all TUs. Output of the fixed version:
rates.hpp
#pragma once
const double kBp = 1e-4;
inline double kScale = 1.0;  // inline variable (C++17): one shared object across TUs
0.0001 1

Interview trap: with internal linkage each TU has its own kBp, so taking its address in two TUs gives two different pointers. Harmless for a constant, but it is why static data does not behave like a singleton across files.

front: What do these print, and why does sizeof(a) inside f give 8 on this build?
back:
#include <iostream>

void f(int a[]) {
    std::cout << "in f: sizeof(a) = " << sizeof(a) << '\n';
}

int main() {
    int a[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    std::cout << "in main: sizeof(a) = " << sizeof(a) << '\n';
    std::cout << "elements = " << sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) << '\n';
    f(a);
}
Output:
in main: sizeof(a) = 20
elements = 5
in f: sizeof(a) = 8

A C array does not carry its size. Passing int a[] to a function passes an int*, and sizeof of a pointer is 8 on this 64-bit build. g++ warns with -Wsizeof-array-argument.

Fix: pass std::span<int> (C++20), which carries the size, or pass the size explicitly. sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) works only where the array type is still visible.

Interview trap: the same expression silently changes meaning when the array is a parameter. Python lists always know their length.

front: std::array<double, 3> has its size as part of the {{c1::type}} and stores its elements inline, so sizeof is 3 × 8 = 24 bytes. std::vector<double> keeps its size at {{c2::run time}} and its elements in {{c3::heap}} memory. The vector object is a small handle, typically three pointers.
back:
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::array<double, 3> a{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};   // N is part of the type
    std::vector<double> v{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};     // size is a run-time value, heap storage
    std::cout << sizeof(a) << ' ' << a.size() << ' ' << v.size() << '\n';
}
Output (sizeof(a), a.size(), v.size()): 24 3 3. Use std::array when the size is fixed and known at compile time; std::vector for anything sized at run time.

front: What does std::string copy = ccy; copy += "USD"; do to ccy? What do ccy == "EUR" and copy == "EURUSD" evaluate to, and what is the pitfall with comparing two const char*?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string ccy = "EUR";
    std::string copy = ccy;          // deep copy: independent of ccy
    copy += "USD";
    std::cout << ccy << ' ' << copy << ' ' << copy.size() << '\n';
    std::cout << (ccy == "EUR") << ' ' << (copy == "EURUSD") << '\n';
}
Output:
EUR EURUSD 6
1 1

  • std::string owns its characters. Assignment makes a deep copy, so ccy is unchanged.
  • == compares contents, not addresses.
  • "EUR" + "USD" does not compile: both operands are const char*. Write std::string("EUR") + "USD".
Interview trap: const char* a compared with == compares pointer values. Two equal literals may or may not share an address, so the result is not specified.

front: What do these three loops print, and which loop modifies dv01?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> dv01{1.0, 2.0};
    for (auto x : dv01) x *= 10;           // x is a copy: dv01 unchanged
    std::cout << dv01[0] << ' ' << dv01[1] << '\n';
    for (auto& x : dv01) x *= 10;          // x is a reference: elements change
    std::cout << dv01[0] << ' ' << dv01[1] << '\n';
    for (const auto& x : dv01) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Output:
1 2
10 20
10 20

  • for (auto x : v) copies each element into x; changes to x are lost.
  • for (auto& x : v) binds x to each element; changes persist.
  • for (const auto& x : v) reads without copying; use it for class types.
Interview trap: for (auto x : bigVector) compiles, runs, and silently copies every element each time. The first loop's assignment has no effect on the vector, which is a common source of bugs when porting Python loops.

front: Compare enum Side { Buy, Sell }; with enum class Tenor { M3, Y1, Y10 };. Show the valid code and the g++ error for int bad = Tenor::Y10;.
back:
#include <iostream>

enum Side { Buy, Sell };              // unscoped: Buy and Sell leak into the enclosing scope
enum class Tenor { M3, Y1, Y10 };     // scoped: must be qualified, no implicit int

int main() {
    int s = Buy;                      // implicit conversion to int: allowed
    Tenor t = Tenor::Y10;
    int ok = static_cast<int>(t);     // explicit conversion
    std::cout << s << ' ' << ok << '\n';
}
Output (s, ok): 0 2

g++ error for the scoped enum:
main.cpp: In function ‘int main()’:
main.cpp:4:22: error: cannot convert ‘Tenor’ to ‘int’ in initialization
    4 |     int bad = Tenor::Y10;   // no implicit conversion from scoped enum to int
      |               ~~~~~~~^~~
      |                      |
      |                      Tenor
Rule: unscoped enumerators leak into the enclosing scope and convert to int implicitly. Scoped enumerators need qualification and convert only with static_cast.

Interview trap: two unscoped enums in one scope that reuse an enumerator name, such as Buy, collide with a compile error. Use enum class for any enum that is part of an interface.

front: A namespace groups names: namespace rates { double df(double r, double t); } is called as {{c1::rates::df}}. Never write {{c2::using namespace std;}} in a header, because it injects every {{c3::std}} name into every file that includes the header.
back: Qualify names in headers (std::vector). A using declaration for a single name, such as using std::string;, is acceptable inside a .cpp file.

front: How do you initialise a struct Bond that has a default notional and a coupon with no default? What does Bond b{}; give for coupon, and why is Bond b; dangerous for scalar members?
back:
struct Bond { double notional = 100.0; double coupon; int freq = 2; }; is an aggregate.
#include <iostream>

struct Bond {
    double notional = 100.0;   // default member initialiser
    double coupon;             // no initialiser: indeterminate if left out
    int    freq = 2;
};

int main() {
    Bond a{1e6, 0.05};         // aggregate initialisation
    Bond b{};                  // value-initialisation: coupon becomes 0.0
    std::cout << a.notional << ' ' << a.coupon << ' ' << a.freq << '\n';
    std::cout << b.notional << ' ' << b.coupon << ' ' << b.freq << '\n';
}
Output:
1e+06 0.05 2
100 0 2

  • Bond a{1e6, 0.05}; sets the first two members; freq takes its default initialiser.
  • Bond b{}; value-initialises the scalars, so coupon is 0.0.
  • Bond c; leaves coupon indeterminate. Reading it is undefined behaviour.
Interview trap: a scalar member without a default initialiser is zero only under braces or value-initialisation. Give every member a default in the struct definition.

front: A function returns a Curve by value, and the object holds a std::vector of pillars. Is the vector deep-copied at each return? How many copies and moves does this program make in C++17 and later?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

struct Curve {
    std::vector<double> pillars;
    static inline int copies = 0, moves = 0;
    Curve() = default;
    explicit Curve(std::vector<double> p) : pillars(std::move(p)) {}
    Curve(const Curve& o) : pillars(o.pillars) { ++copies; }
    Curve(Curve&& o) noexcept : pillars(std::move(o.pillars)) { ++moves; }
};

Curve bootstrap() {
    return Curve{std::vector<double>{0.5, 1.0, 2.0}};   // prvalue: guaranteed elision in C++17
}

int main() {
    Curve c = bootstrap();
    std::cout << "copies=" << Curve::copies << " moves=" << Curve::moves
              << " pillars=" << c.pillars.size() << '\n';
}
Output: copies=0 moves=0 pillars=3

Answer: no copies, no moves. return Curve{...}; returns a prvalue, and since C++17 the object is constructed directly in the caller's storage (guaranteed copy elision). Returning a named local (return c;) is elided in practice (NRVO) and, when it is not, is treated as a move.

Interview trap: return std::move(c); on a local prevents the elision and forces a move. Return the name plainly.

front: What does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to in C++, and why? Print the sum with 17 significant digits and explain the output.
back:
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    double a = 0.1 + 0.2;
    std::cout << std::setprecision(17) << a << '\n';
    std::cout << (a == 0.3) << '\n';
    std::cout << std::setprecision(6) << a << '\n';
}
Output:
0.30000000000000004
0
0.3

Why: double is IEEE 754 binary64: a 53-bit significand, so 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are not exact. The sum rounds to the neighbouring representable value, which is not the double nearest to 0.3. digits10 is 15, which is the guaranteed decimal precision; 17 digits are needed to round-trip any double.

Interview trap: never test doubles with == for a zero or reconciliation check. The same effect breaks P&L tie-outs and "equal" strike checks when values come from different summation orders.

front: Write a scale-aware comparison of doubles. What are epsilon(), min() (not lowest()), max() and digits10 for double? Why does a NaN break a plain if (px < 0) reject check?
back:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <limits>

bool nearly_equal(double a, double b, double rel = 1e-12, double abs_tol = 1e-14) {
    return std::abs(a - b) <= std::max(abs_tol, rel * std::max(std::abs(a), std::abs(b)));
}

int main() {
    using L = std::numeric_limits<double>;
    std::cout << "epsilon  " << L::epsilon() << '\n';
    std::cout << "min      " << L::min() << '\n';
    std::cout << "max      " << L::max() << '\n';
    std::cout << "digits10 " << L::digits10 << '\n';
    double nan = L::quiet_NaN();
    std::cout << "nan==nan " << (nan == nan) << '\n';
    std::cout << "isnan    " << std::isnan(nan) << '\n';
    std::cout << "nearly_equal(0.1+0.2, 0.3) = " << nearly_equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) << '\n';
    std::cout << "nearly_equal(1.0, 1.1)     = " << nearly_equal(1.0, 1.1) << '\n';
}
Output:
epsilon 2.22045e-16
min 2.22507e-308
max 1.79769e+308
digits10 15
nan==nan 0
isnan 1
nearly_equal(0.1+0.2, 0.3) = 1
nearly_equal(1.0, 1.1) = 0

  • epsilon() is the gap between 1.0 and the next representable double, about 2.2e-16.
  • min() is the smallest positive normal value; lowest() is the most negative finite value.
  • The helper combines an absolute and a relative tolerance. Relative alone fails near zero, where the abs term takes over.
  • NaN fails every ordered comparison and is not equal to itself. if (px < 0) lets NaN through. Write if (!(px >= 0)) or test with std::isnan.
Interview trap: a validation that uses x < 0 to reject bad inputs accepts NaN silently. Financial data pipelines produce NaN from 0/0 in a zero-volume bucket, so the check has to be written to catch it.

front: Define undefined behaviour in C++. Why is "it crashes" the wrong mental model? Name the four classic examples this module covers.
back:
Definition: the standard places no requirement on what happens. The compiler may assume the event never occurs and optimise on that basis. The program can print the right answer, a wrong one, crash, or behave differently at another optimisation level or on another compiler.

Four classic examples:
  1. Reading an uninitialised automatic variable.
  2. Accessing an element outside an array or vector.
  3. Signed integer overflow.
  4. Using memory after it has been freed (dangling pointer or reference).
Other examples include data races and strict-aliasing violations.

Interview trap: code that behaves differently at -O0 and -O2 usually contains UB; the optimiser is not the bug. Run it under sanitizers to find the cause.

front: This program has a bug. What is it, what does g++ -Wall -Wextra -O2 report, and what can you say about the number it prints? int total; for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) total += i; std::cout << total;
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int total;                                // indeterminate value
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) total += i;   // reads an uninitialised object: UB
    std::cout << total << '\n';
}
g++ warning:
main.cpp: In function ‘int main()’:
main.cpp:5:39: warning: ‘total’ is used uninitialized [-Wuninitialized]
    5 |     for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) total += i;   // reads an uninitialised object: UB
      |                                 ~~~~~~^~~~
main.cpp:4:9: note: ‘total’ was declared here
    4 |     int total;                                // indeterminate value
      |         ^~~~~
Output on this run: 3. Reading total before it is initialised is undefined behaviour, so this value is not guaranteed; it happened to be 0 before the loop on this build.

Fix: int total = 0; or int total{};.

Interview trap: local scalars are not zeroed in C++, unlike Python. UBSan does not catch this read; use Valgrind memcheck or Clang's MemorySanitizer.

front: This loop indexes past the end of a vector. Predict what it does, and what does AddressSanitizer report when you compile with -fsanitize=address -g -O1?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> pillars{0.25, 0.5, 1.0};
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= 3; ++i)     // off by one: i == 3 is past the end
        sum += pillars[i];
    std::cout << sum << '\n';
}
Without the sanitizer at -O2 the program printed 1.75: the out-of-bounds read returned a value that happened to be harmless, which is undefined behaviour.

AddressSanitizer report (first line, address elided):
==8605==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow at pc 0x55aaf73d0621 bp 0x7ffee20b5430 sp 0x7ffee20b5420
The report points at main.cpp:8, the line sum += pillars[i];.

Fix: loop with i < pillars.size(), use a range-for, or use pillars.at(i), which throws std::out_of_range.

Interview trap: operator[] never checks bounds. The compiler accepts pillars[3] without a diagnostic.

front: Why does x + 1 with x = INT_MAX break a program, and what does UBSan report? The function is int bump(int x) { return x + 1; }; the value is held in a volatile so the compiler cannot fold it.
back:
#include <climits>
#include <iostream>

int bump(int x) { return x + 1; }       // signed overflow is undefined behaviour

int main() {
    volatile int v = INT_MAX;           // volatile: keep the value opaque to the compiler
    std::cout << bump(v) << '\n';
}
Output without UBSan (-O2): -2147483648. The result wrapped, but the standard does not promise that.

UBSan report (compiled with -fsanitize=undefined):
main.cpp:4:30: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 2147483647 + 1 cannot be represented in type 'int'
Rule: signed overflow is undefined behaviour; unsigned overflow wraps by definition. The compiler may therefore reason as if x + 1 > x is always true for an int.

Interview trap: a risk model that accumulates a signed 32-bit counter of trades or basis points can overflow silently at -O2. Use std::int64_t, or check before adding.

front: With the same kind of code as before, what does this program print at -O2 and why? bool always_bigger(int x) { return x + 1 > x; } is called with INT_MAX (through a volatile).
back:
#include <iostream>

bool always_bigger(int x) { return x + 1 > x; }   // compiler may assume no overflow

int main() {
    volatile int v = 2147483647;
    std::cout << always_bigger(v) << '\n';
}
Output: 1. For x = INT_MAX the comparison is false under wrap-around, but g++ at -O2 compiled the function to return true.

Why: because signed overflow is undefined, the optimiser may assume x + 1 > x holds for every int, and folds the test away. The code is correct only under a rule the standard does not give you.

Interview trap: overflow guards written as if (x + 1 < x) are removed by the optimiser. Test before the operation: if (x > INT_MAX - 1), or use __builtin_add_overflow.

front: Why does view[1] produce a garbage value here, even though view was assigned before free_buf ran? Show the AddressSanitizer report type and the fix.
back:
buf.cpp
#include <cstdlib>
double* make_buf() { return new double[3]{0.5, 1.0, 2.0}; }   // separate TU: no elision
void free_buf(double* p) { delete[] p; }
main.cpp
#include <iostream>
double* make_buf();
void free_buf(double* p);
int main() {
    double* p = make_buf();
    double* view = p;               // non-owning alias
    free_buf(p);                    // memory released here
    std::cout << view[1] << '\n';   // use after free
}
Without the sanitizer, -O2 printed an arbitrary value (one run: -3.61871e-152; the value changes between runs). With -fsanitize=address:
==8686==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free at pc 0x56464cfb932c bp 0x7ffd7e84a3a0 sp 0x7ffd7e84a390
Cause: view is a non-owning raw pointer. Freeing the memory invalidates every alias, and the allocator may reuse it.

Fix: own the buffer with a std::vector<double> or std::unique_ptr<double[]>; for a non-owning view use std::span, which does not prevent the owner from being freed.

Interview trap: a single-file version of this code was constant-folded at -O2 and printed 1.0 with no sanitizer report. A dangling pointer can look correct until the optimiser or the allocator changes.

front: Compile with {{c1::-fsanitize=address,undefined}} to catch heap and stack buffer overflows, use-after-free and leaks with AddressSanitizer, and {{c2::signed overflow, null dereference and misaligned access}} with UBSan. An uninitialised read is {{c3::not}} caught by UBSan: use Valgrind memcheck or Clang's MemorySanitizer.
back: Build with -O1 -g for readable stack traces. The combination compiles and runs in this environment (g++ 13). Sanitizers add overhead; use them in tests and debug builds, not for production timing. Note: leak detection is part of AddressSanitizer on Linux.

front: Two .cpp files each define a different struct Quote with a mid() member. Both compile and link. What goes wrong, and what does this build print for mid_a(1, 3) and mid_b(1, 3) at -O0?
back:
quote_a.cpp
struct Quote {
    double bid, ask;
    [[gnu::noinline]] double mid() const { return 0.5 * (bid + ask); }
};
double mid_a(double b, double a) { Quote q{b, a}; return q.mid(); }
quote_b.cpp
struct Quote {                       // same class name, different definition
    double bid, ask;
    [[gnu::noinline]] double mid() const { return bid; }
};
double mid_b(double b, double a) { Quote q{b, a}; return q.mid(); }
main.cpp
#include <iostream>
double mid_a(double, double);
double mid_b(double, double);
int main() {
    std::cout << mid_a(1.0, 3.0) << ' ' << mid_b(1.0, 3.0) << '\n';
}
Output at -O0: 2 2. mid_b should give 1. Output at -O2: 2 1, which is correct only because the optimiser inlined the calls.

Why: the two Quote::mid() const functions have the same mangled name. The linker keeps one definition, so one function silently replaces the other. This is an ODR violation between class definitions; the linker has no way to see it.

Fix: put each internal type in an unnamed namespace, or give it a unique name. Never define one class name two ways in one program.

Interview trap: g++ reports ODR violations only with -flto (-Wodr). Without it the test suite can pass at one optimisation level and fail at another.
